A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same UGPP problem and UGPrompt framework despite the changed title. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original graph and node classification experiments, distribution-shift evaluations, ablations, and embedding analyses in the main text and appendix.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds benchmark comparisons, transfer experiments, runtime measurements, and pseudo-label reliability diagnostics.

M1.justification: The core unsupervised architecture and three losses remain unchanged. The few-shot pseudo-label loss changes from summing over the full batch B in v1 Equation 8 to unlabeled samples Su in v2 Section 4.4. Algorithm 2's body also switches from returning scores to argmax labels, although its output header still says scores. The PDFs do not establish corresponding implementation changes or reruns.

E1.justification: v2 adds BBBP and BACE molecular graph datasets and Cornell, Texas, and Wisconsin node datasets while retaining the original coverage. It also adds cross-dataset transfer, a stress test with reindexed target categories, and evaluation without distribution shift (Section 4.5 and Appendix A.6.3), substantially broadening the tested populations and scenarios.

E2.justification: Beyond the retained comparators, v2 evaluates DAGPrompt, PRONOG, and GCOPE in Tables 9–10 and SOGA and GraphCTA in Table 14. The SFDA comparators are explicitly adapted to freeze their encoders and train their prediction heads; these are not evaluations of unrestricted full-model adaptation.

E3.justification: v2 introduces sorted source/target partitions with graded shift severity, category reindexing with a three-output frozen head, GraphGPS and GATv2 backbones, and an additional comparison allowing supervised baselines to fine-tune their decoders. New diagnostics measure MMD, pseudo-label accuracy, ECE, and runtime. The original main-experiment splits and tuning grids are retained.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained ablations and embedding analysis, v2 adds graded-shift sensitivity, cross-dataset and category-transfer stress tests, source-performance retention, no-shift controls, computational-cost analysis, MMD diagnostics, and confidence-threshold/calibration analysis. These test robustness and mechanism questions largely unexamined in v1.

E5.justification: Both versions specify 10 dataset seeds and five model initializations per seed, totaling 50 runs, and mix results with ± reporting and point estimates. No new confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty-estimation procedures are specified. The added calibration study evaluates predictive reliability rather than changing sampling-uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results for new datasets, comparators, transfer settings, runtime, and reliability diagnostics; for example, Table 1 newly reports UGPrompt's GCN BACE F1 as 64.6±1.9. Most original scores remain. One retained entry changes: GraphPrompt's 50%-label CiteSeer clustering-shift IMP moves from +1.6 in v1 Table 7 to -1.6 in v2 Table 12 despite unchanged F1 values.

T1.justification: The few-shot loss definition changes its summation domain from B to Su and its confidence comparison from strict to inclusive (v1 Equation 8; v2 Section 4.4). The formal UGPP assumptions, core unsupervised objectives, and complexity bound otherwise remain equivalent. No new theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The central UGPP formulation and fully unsupervised frozen-GNN prompting contributions remain. v2's introduction strengthens the comparative claim from outperforming baselines 'in most cases' to consistently outperforming methods with full label access. Its conclusion also explicitly qualifies applicability to a shared source/target label space.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly interprets adversarial regularization as target-side stabilization, with source compatibility supplied indirectly by the frozen model and confidence filtering. It adds substantive discussion of confirmation bias, calibration, access to unlabeled data, computational tradeoffs, and the distinction from LLM reasoning. The new limitations paragraph explains why a frozen head cannot generally accommodate new target classes.

D1.justification: v2 adds measured training and inference times with evaluated node counts in Table 21 and clarifies validation-based disabling of ineffective regularizers. The PyTorch implementation, RTX 3090 hardware, principal hyperparameter grids, and code-access statement are retained. These are limited additions to technical documentation.

R1.justification: v1 distinguishes UGPP from source-free adaptation mainly in an appendix. v2 explicitly positions it as a restrictive prompting instance within SFDA in the introduction and problem formulation. It substantially expands engagement with recent graph prompting, graph SFDA, and PEFT through DAGPrompt, PRONOG, GCOPE, SOGA, GraphCTA, and LoRA, beyond merely relocating related work.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, and introduction are substantially rewritten around source-free, parameter-efficient adaptation. Related work moves from v1 Section 2 to v2 Appendix A.1, the experimental and appendix organization expands, and terminology systematically distinguishes 'source-trained' from general 'pre-trained' models. These changes substantially revise the narrative and structure.

P2.justification: Tables 1–2 expand with new dataset columns, Figure 2 is redrawn with logarithmic axes, revised legends, and additional datasets, and numerous new comparisons and diagnostics receive dedicated tables. Journal formatting changes typography, margins, headers, and table styling. The original framework, embedding, and higher-label-budget figures are largely retained.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens assessment of the central adaptation claim: comparisons with decoder-finetuned prompting and adapted SFDA methods address v1's restricted comparison regime, while MMD and calibration diagnostics test previously mostly intuitive mechanism arguments. Explicit label-space limitations improve applicability guidance. These gains outweigh remaining weaknesses: superiority language exceeds the new evidence—DAGPrompt leads on five of seven datasets in Table 10—and v2 introduces an inconsistent IMP sign in Table 12.
